Explore how late-layer representations can be used for steering and safety applications.
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) architectures are often described as functionally hierarchical: Early layers process syntax, middle layers begin to parse semantics, and late layers integrate information. The present work revisits these ideas. This research submits simple texts to an LLM (e.g., "A church and organ") and extracts the resulting activations. Then, for each layer, support vector machines and ridge regressions are fit to predict a text's label and thus examine whether a given layer encodes some information. Analyses using a small model (Llama-3.2-3b; 28 layers) partly bolster the common hierarchical perspective: Item-level semantics are most strongly represented early (layers 2-7), then two-item relations (layers 8-12), and then four-item analogies (layers 10-15). Afterward, the representation of items and simple relations gradually decreases in deeper layers that focus on more global information. However, several findings run counter to a steady hierarchy view: First, although deep layers can represent document-wide abstractions, deep layers also compress information from early portions of the context window without meaningful abstraction. Second, when examining a larger model (Llama-3.3-70b-Instruct), stark fluctuations in abstraction level appear: As depth increases, two-item relations and four-item analogies initially increase in their representation, then markedly decrease, and afterward increase again momentarily. This peculiar pattern consistently emerges across several experiments. Third, another emergent effect of scaling is coordination between the attention mechanisms of adjacent layers. Across multiple experiments using the larger model, adjacent layers fluctuate between what information they each specialize in representing. In sum, an abstraction hierarchy often manifests across layers, but large models also deviate from this structure in curious ways.

papers.title: Vocabulary embeddings organize linguistic structure early in language model training
papers.research_question: How are the input vocabulary representations of language models structured, and how and when does this structure evolve over training?
papers.core_contribution: Vocabulary embeddings quickly converge to high correlations with semantic and syntactic features during training, with high-frequency and function words converging faster than low-frequency words, which retain alignment with their random initializations.
papers.conclusion: Vocabulary embeddings rapidly organize linguistic structure early in training, with frequency and function playing distinct roles, motivating deeper study of how embedding evolution facilitates capability gains.
papers.key_findings:
During training, vocabulary embedding geometry quickly converges to high correlations with semantic and syntactic features.
Embeddings of high-frequency and function words converge to their final vectors faster than lexical and low-frequency words.
Low-frequency words retain some alignment with the bias in their random initializations, while high-frequency words completely shed initialization biases.
Embeddings continue to change after linguistic features stabilize, with rare words moving closer to their morphological inflections.
The correlation between input and output embeddings peaks when linguistic features stabilize.
future_direction: Understanding why OLMo attains stronger part-of-speech correlations than Pythia.
Understanding the interactions of combined linguistic features in model embeddings.
Understanding the dynamics and geometry of subword tokens.
Studying how the evolution of vocabulary geometry may facilitate specific capability gains during model training.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) work by manipulating the geometry of input embedding vectors over multiple layers. Here, we ask: how are the input vocabulary representations of language models structured, and how and when does this structure evolve over training? To answer this question, we use representational similarity analysis, running a suite of experiments that correlate the geometric structure of the input embeddings and output embeddings of two open-source models (Pythia 12B and OLMo 7B) with semantic, syntactic, and frequency-based metrics over the course of training. Our key findings are as follows: 1) During training, the vocabulary embedding geometry quickly converges to high correlations with a suite of semantic and syntactic features; 2) Embeddings of high-frequency and function words (e.g., "the," "of") converge to their final vectors faster than lexical and low-frequency words, which retain some alignment with the bias in their random initializations. These findings help map the dynamic trajectory by which input embeddings organize around linguistic structure, revealing distinct roles for word frequency and function. Our findings motivate a deeper study of how the evolution of vocabulary geometry may facilitate specific capability gains during model training.

papers.title: Diverging views on the role of structured representations in linguistics and language modeling
papers.research_question: How do language models compare to human language processing in terms of structured representations, and what is their role in the science of language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that language models struggle with structured representations central to human language, and suggests that for language models to be effective models of language, structured representations must be incorporated as computational objects.
papers.conclusion: Language models need to conceptualize structured representations as computational objects to better align with human language and contribute to the science of language.
papers.key_findings:
Language models trained on next-word prediction may not learn structure-dependent representations necessary for human language.
Models like ChatGPT show insensitivity to Binding Principle C, incorrectly allowing co-reference in prohibited contexts.
Language models do not make a qualitative distinction between possible and impossible languages, treating them similarly unlike humans.
The internal representational infrastructure for possible and impossible languages overlaps in models, indicating no fundamental difference.
Incorporating structured representations as primary computational targets could enhance language models' utility as models of language.
future_direction: Incorporate structured representations as computational objects in language modeling.
papers.abstract: Recent years have seen dramatic advances in the linguistic abilities of language models, leading some authors to argue that they can be treated as models of language. Against this background, we provide a cognitive perspective on the place of language models in the science of language, with a particular focus on the role of structured representations. Evidence from linguistics, psychology and cognitive neuroscience shows that structured representations occupy a central place in the human mind. Structured representations constrain how linguistic forms map onto meanings, thereby determining the boundaries of possible human languages. In language modeling, instead, the place of structured representations is often peripheral. They are seen as optional end point of modeling, to be induced as a consequence of the objective the model tries to optimize – that is, next-word prediction. Because structured relations and representations are not necessarily useful for predicting the next word in a sequence, it is not guaranteed that the model’s internal organization will come to encode those representations. Indeed, contemporary language models struggle to use structured representations functionally to map form onto meaning, and to determine whether they should consider their input as a possible human language or not. Building on classic insights in linguistics and (computational) cognitive science, we suggest that any use of language models as models of language requires conceptualizing the role of structured representations as computational objects.

papers.title: What Does BERT Learn about the Structure of Language?
papers.research_question: What linguistic structure does BERT learn? Specifically, can we unveil the representations learned by BERT to proto-linguistics structures?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that BERT captures hierarchical linguistic structure, with surface features in lower layers, syntactic in middle, and semantic in higher layers, and that it uses deeper layers for long-distance dependencies and implicitly captures tree-like structures.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that BERT captures structural properties of English language, with a hierarchy of linguistic signals and compositional modeling that parallels traditional syntactic analysis.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers, which gets diluted in higher layers.
BERT embeds a rich hierarchy of linguistic signals: surface information at the bottom, syntactic in the middle, and semantic at the top.
BERT requires deeper layers to handle long-distance dependency information, such as subject-verb agreement with more attractors.
BERT implicitly implements a tree-based compositional scheme, as shown by Tensor Product Decomposition Networks (TPDN) approximating BERT's representations.
The untrained version of BERT in higher layers outperforms the trained version in predicting sentence length, indicating that training trades off basic surface features for more complex information.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to English and may not generalize to other languages or noisy user-generated content.
future_direction: Investigating if the results transfer to other domains with higher syntactic variability, such as noisy user-generated content or morphologically-rich languages.
papers.abstract: BERT is a recent language representation model that has surprisingly performed well in diverse language understanding benchmarks. This result indicates the possibility that BERT networks capture structural information about language. In this work, we provide novel support for this claim by performing a series of experiments to unpack the elements of English language structure learned by BERT. We first show that BERT's phrasal representation captures phrase-level information in the lower layers. We also show that BERT's intermediate layers encode a rich hierarchy of linguistic information, with surface features at the bottom, syntactic features in the middle and semantic features at the top. BERT turns out to require deeper layers when long-distance dependency information is required, e.g. to track subjectverb agreement. Finally, we show that BERT representations capture linguistic information in a compositional way that mimics classical, tree-like structures.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Correlating Neural and Symbolic Representations of Language
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the correspondence between neural activation patterns and symbolic structures such as syntax trees? Do neural models encode syntactic information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two RSA-based methods (Structured RSA and RSA_REGRESS) for correlating neural and symbolic representations, validates them on synthetic language, and applies them to show that neural models encode syntactic information, with syntax most salient in intermediate layers of BERT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods are effective for correlating neural and symbolic representations and reveal that neural models encode syntactic information, with the highest encoding in intermediate layers.
papers.key_findings:
On synthetic language, the methods show the expected pattern: encoders trained on tasks requiring syntactic structure show higher correlation with tree kernel similarities.
Both Infersent and BERT encode syntactic information, with trained models showing higher correlation than random models.
In BERT, syntactic information peaks in intermediate layers (layers 15-22) and declines in later layers.
Randomly initialized models exhibit non-random activation patterns that correlate negatively with tree kernel similarities, indicating that learning must overcome initial biases.
RSA_REGRESS is less sensitive to the tree kernel discounting parameter λ than standard RSA.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other symbolic representations such as dependency trees or Abstract Meaning Representations.
papers.abstract: Analysis methods which enable us to better understand the representations and functioning of neural models of language are increasingly needed as deep learning becomes the dominant approach in NLP. Here we present two methods based on Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Tree Kernels (TK) which allow us to directly quantify how strongly the information encoded in neural activation patterns corresponds to information represented by symbolic structures such as syntax trees. We first validate our methods on the case of a simple synthetic language for arithmetic expressions with clearly defined syntax and semantics, and show that they exhibit the expected pattern of results. We then apply our methods to correlate neural representations of English sentences with their constituency parse trees.

papers.title: Understanding the role of FFNs in driving multilingual behaviour in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) in large language models drive multilingual behavior, and what are the patterns of multilingual processing across layers and model sizes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the metric 'activation flatness' and analyzes FFN sublayers (detectors and combinators) to reveal distinct patterns of multilingual processing, identifying the phenomenon of 'over-layerization' where increasing layer depth without other adjustments can degrade performance.
papers.conclusion: The analysis reveals distinct patterns in FFN sublayers for multilingual processing, with detectors becoming more peaked and language-specific in later layers, and combinators showing multilingual behavior in middle layers, while also identifying over-layerization in certain model configurations.
papers.key_findings:
FFN representations are more sparse near the input and output layers across all models.
Detector activations become more peaked (less flat) through the layers, while combinator activations show a distinct drop in flatness around layer 20 regardless of model size.
Early detector layers are multilingual and process shallow features, becoming more language-specific near the output.
Combinator layers are mostly multilingual in the middle layers, with the final layers becoming language-specific, especially in larger models.
The 2.9B parameter model exhibits 'over-layerization', where increased layer depth without corresponding adjustments leads to degraded generation quality compared to the 7.5B model.
papers.limitation:
The analysis relies only on model snapshots (activations), which does not fully capture the complexities of LLMs; probing tasks or attention matrices could provide a more comprehensive understanding.
The investigation is limited to the XGLM model family, and findings may not generalize to other LLM architectures or implementations.
The analysis is limited to a set of predefined languages and test sets, which may not fully represent linguistic diversity.
future_direction: Investigate whether flatter activation patterns are easier to adapt in QLoRA fine-tuning.
Extend the analysis to more languages and explore cross-linguistic variation in more detail.
papers.abstract: Multilingualism in Large Language Models (LLMs) is an yet under-explored area. In this paper, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the multilingual capabilities of a family of a Large Language Model, examining its architecture, activation patterns, and processing mechanisms across languages. We introduce novel metrics to probe the model's multilingual behaviour at different layers and shed light on the impact of architectural choices on multilingual processing. Our findings reveal different patterns of multilinugal processing in the sublayers of Feed-Forward Networks of the models. Furthermore, we uncover the phenomenon of "over-layerization" in certain model configurations, where increasing layer depth without corresponding adjustments to other parameters may degrade model performance. Through comparisons within and across languages, we demonstrate the interplay between model architecture, layer depth, and multilingual processing capabilities of LLMs trained on multiple languages.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: DOCS: Quantifying Weight Similarity for Deeper Insights into Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantitatively assess the similarity between weight matrices in Large Language Models to gain deeper insights into their complex architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DOCS, a novel index for quantifying weight similarity in LLMs that effectively differentiates orthogonal matrices, and uses it to uncover patterns such as high similarity between adjacent layers and the existence of layer clusters.
papers.conclusion: DOCS provides an effective measure for weight similarity, revealing structural patterns in LLMs that can inform model design and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Neighboring transformer layers exhibit high weight similarity.
Clusters of similar transformer layers exist within LLMs.
Weight similarity decreases with increasing layer distance.
Base and instruction-tuned models retain high weight similarity, indicating foundational knowledge is preserved.
In Mixture-of-Experts models, some experts are distinct from others, suggesting specialization.
future_direction: Applying DOCS to guide model compression, architecture design, and fine-tuning strategies.
Leveraging cluster structures for inductive biases during supervised fine-tuning.
Exploring the universality of cluster patterns across different models and training regimes.
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel index, the Distribution of Cosine Similarity (DOCS), for quantitatively assessing the similarity between weight matrices in Large Language Models (LLMs), aiming to facilitate the analysis of their complex architectures. Leveraging DOCS, our analysis uncovers intriguing patterns in the latest open-source LLMs: adjacent layers frequently exhibit high weight similarity and tend to form clusters, suggesting depth-wise functional specialization. Additionally, we prove that DOCS is theoretically effective in quantifying similarity for orthogonal matrices, a crucial aspect given the prevalence of orthogonal initializations in LLMs. This research contributes to a deeper understanding of LLM architecture and behavior, offering tools with potential implications for developing more efficient and interpretable models.

papers.title: Low-Dimensional Structure in the Space of Language Representations is\n Reflected in Brain Responses
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks, and is this low-dimensional structure reflected in human brain responses to natural language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language representations from various models and tasks lie in a low-dimensional space, and that this structure can predict how well each representation maps to brain responses, revealing a hierarchy in the brain's language processing.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations is reflected in the brain, and the representation embedding method captures this structure, linking computational models to neural processing.
papers.key_findings:
The space of language representations has a low-dimensional structure, with the first dimension explaining 22% of variance.
Language model layers follow a trajectory from word embeddings to next-word embeddings, with syntactic and semantic tasks clustering in the middle.
The first dimension of the representation embedding space corresponds to a hierarchy in the brain's language processing, from auditory cortex to higher-level semantic areas.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain responses in different regions.
Some pairs of representations are difficult to distinguish based on brain responses, such as GloVe and its next-word embedding due to fMRI temporal imprecision.
papers.limitation: The temporal imprecision of fMRI data limits the ability to distinguish between representations that are close in time, such as GloVe and its next-word embedding.
papers.abstract:
How related are the representations learned by neural language models,
translation models, and language tagging tasks? We answer this question by
adapting an encoder-decoder transfer learning method from computer vision to
investigate the structure among 100 different feature spaces extracted from
hidden representations of various networks trained on language tasks. This
method reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and
translation models smoothly interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic and
semantic tasks, and future word embeddings. We call this low-dimensional
structure a language representation embedding because it encodes the
relationships between representations needed to process language for a variety
of NLP tasks. We find that this representation embedding can predict how well
each individual feature space maps to human brain responses to natural language
stimuli recorded using fMRI. Additionally, we find that the principal dimension
of this structure can be used to create a metric which highlights the brain's
natural language processing hierarchy. This suggests that the embedding
captures some part of the brain's natural language representation structure.

papers.title: Conceptual structure coheres in human cognition but not in large language models
papers.research_question: Does conceptual structure in large language models cohere across different probing tasks as it does in humans, or do human and LLM conceptual representations differ in robustness?
papers.core_contribution: Human conceptual structure is robust across different tasks and cultures, but large language models exhibit less coherence in conceptual structure across different probing tasks, indicating a lack of a stable conceptual core.
papers.conclusion: Human conceptual structure is robust to differences in task, language, and culture, while contemporary LLMs lack such coherence, highlighting a fundamental difference between human cognition and current machine language models.
papers.key_findings:
Human conceptual structure estimates from three different tasks (feature listing, triadic comparisons, pairwise ratings) are highly coherent (squared Procrustes correlations between 0.72 and 0.96).
LLM conceptual structure estimates vary depending on the probing task; for GPT-3, the squared Procrustes correlations between different task embeddings are lower (e.g., 0.72 between feature listing and triplet, 0.47 between feature listing and pairwise, 0.25 between triplet and pairwise).
LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: Correspondence between the layered structure of deep language models and temporal structure of natural language processing in the human brain
papers.research_question: Does the layered hierarchy of deep language models (DLMs) correspond to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain? Specifically, is there a correlation between DLM layer depth and the time at which layers are most predictive of human brain activity?
papers.core_contribution: The layered hierarchy of deep language models (specifically GPT2-XL) corresponds to the temporal dynamics of language comprehension in the human brain, with early layers predicting early neural responses and later layers predicting later responses in high-order language areas.
papers.conclusion: The internal sequence of computations across layers in deep language models models the temporal hierarchy of language comprehension in the human brain, providing evidence for shared computational principles between DLMs and the brain.
papers.key_findings:
There is a strong positive correlation (Pearson r=0.85 in IFG) between DLM layer depth and the time of peak encoding performance in high-order language areas (IFG, TP, aSTG).
Intermediate layers of GPT2-XL (e.g., layer 22 in IFG) provide the best overall prediction of neural activity across language areas, forming an inverted U-shaped curve.
For predictable words, the temporal sequence is clear; for unpredictable words, the pattern is weaker and early layers shift to later lags (around 300ms) in IFG.
The temporal progression timescale increases along the ventral linguistic hierarchy, with the largest within-ROI temporal separation in the Temporal Pole (over 500 ms).
The observed lag-layer correlation is due to nonlinear transformations in the DLM, as linear interpolations between first and last layer embeddings yield significantly lower correlations.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a single DLM (GPT2-XL) and a single narrative stimulus, limiting generalizability.
The temporal resolution of the ECoG measurements, although high, was binned at 50 ms, which may not disambiguate layers that peak at similar times.
The hierarchical structure of DLMs is spatial, while that of the brain is spatiotemporal, representing a fundamental architectural difference.
future_direction: Explore other model architectures (e.g., recurrent, convolutional, or models with explicit temporal dynamics) to see if they better capture brain dynamics.
Use longer contexts and more diverse stimuli to test the robustness of the layer-time correspondence.
Investigate how DLMs might be augmented (e.g., with recurrence or explicit temporal hierarchies) to better model the brain's spatiotemporal language processing.
papers.abstract: Abstract Deep language models (DLMs) provide a novel computational paradigm for how the brain processes natural language. Unlike symbolic, rule-based models described in psycholinguistics, DLMs encode words and their context as continuous numerical vectors. These “embeddings” are constructed by a sequence of computations organized in “layers” to ultimately capture surprisingly sophisticated representations of linguistic structures. How does this layered hierarchy map onto the human brain during natural language comprehension? In this study, we used electrocorticography (ECoG) to record neural activity in language areas along the superior temporal gyrus and inferior frontal gyrus while human participants listened to a 30-minute spoken narrative. We supplied this same narrative to a high-performing DLM (GPT2-XL) and extracted the contextual embeddings for each word in the story across all 48 layers of the model. We next trained a set of linear encoding models to predict the temporally-evolving neural activity from the embeddings at each layer. We found a striking correspondence between the layer-by-layer sequence of embeddings from GPT2-XL and the temporal sequence of neural activity in language areas. In addition, we found evidence for the gradual accumulation of recurrent information along the linguistic processing hierarchy. However, we also noticed additional neural processes in the brain, but not in DLMs, during the processing of surprising (unpredictable) words. These findings point to a connection between human language processing and DLMs where the layer-by-layer accumulation of contextual information in DLM embeddings matches the temporal dynamics of neural activity in high-order language areas.

papers.title: From Tokens to Words: On the Inner Lexicon of LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs encode words internally from sub-word tokens, and if so, how.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally detokenize sub-word tokens into whole-word representations in early to middle layers via an inner lexicon, enabling vocabulary expansion without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The work unravels the word detokenization process in LLMs, showing it occurs in early to middle layers and enables practical applications for optimizing tokenization and inference costs.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can distinguish words from nonwords, with the distinction emerging in early to middle layers.
The last token of a word (even if split) can be decoded as the full word, indicating an inner lexicon.
FFN layers are crucial for retrieving full-word representations from the inner lexicon.
Attention patterns show early layers aggregate sub-word tokens, then later layers ignore them as the full word representation forms.
The inner lexicon can be used to expand the model's vocabulary without fine-tuning, reducing token count and maintaining performance.
papers.limitation:
22.6% of multi-token words are never successfully decoded, indicating the inner lexicon does not cover all words.
Vocabulary expansion success rate is lower for morphologically rich languages like Arabic (16%).
papers.abstract: Natural language is composed of words, but modern large language models (LLMs) process sub-words as input. A natural question raised by this discrepancy is whether LLMs encode words internally, and if so how. We present evidence that LLMs engage in an intrinsic detokenization process, where sub-word sequences are combined into coherent whole-word representations at their last token. Our experiments show that this process primarily takes place within the early and middle layers of the model. We further demonstrate its robustness to arbitrary splits (e.g., "cats" to "ca" and "ts"), typos, and importantly-to out-of-vocabulary words: when feeding the last token internal representations of such words to the model as input, it can "understand" them as the complete word despite never seeing such representations as input during training. Our findings suggest that LLMs maintain a latent vocabulary beyond the tokenizer's scope. These insights provide a practical, finetuning-free application for expanding the vocabulary of pre-trained models. By enabling the addition of new vocabulary words, we reduce input length and inference iterations, which reduces both space and model latency, with little to no loss in model accuracy.

papers.title: Linguistics and Human Brain: A Perspective of Computational Neuroscience
papers.research_question: How can computational neuroscience bridge the methodological gap between linguistics and neuroscience to elucidate the language-brain relationship?
papers.core_contribution: This review synthesizes interdisciplinary progress from a computational neuroscience perspective, outlining how it formalizes linguistic theories into testable models and uses large language models to advance model-brain alignment for understanding language processing.
papers.conclusion: This work aims to advance a comprehensive, mechanistic understanding of the language-brain relationship and promote computational neuroscience as a generative theoretical framework for testable neuro-computational accounts of language.
papers.key_findings:
Cross-modal interactions between language and perceptual systems (e.g., vision, music) exist and are partially captured by multimodal large models, providing tools for studying semantic coding.
Inter-brain neural coupling during communication shows alignment between speaker and listener neural systems, with coupling strength increasing with shared semantic representations.
Hierarchical computation in large language models aligns with brain processing, but differences exist, prompting debate on whether models implement genuine hierarchical computation or statistical learning.
Large language models and humans show similar sensitivities in learning strategies, such as in-context learning, revealing parallels in adaptive language processing.
Language plasticity in the brain, including acquisition and adaptation, can be studied through model-brain alignment, offering insights into neural mechanisms of learning and recovery.
papers.limitation:
Functional alignment without structural homology
Constraints on real-time validation
Biased research coverage
Narrow evaluation metrics
future_direction: Improving biological plausibility via spiking neural network–based language models
Developing cognitive-level alignment frameworks integrating memory, causality, and metacognition
Extending clinical applications and brain–computer interface applications
papers.abstract: Elucidating the language-brain relationship requires bridging the methodological gap between the abstract theoretical frameworks of linguistics and the empirical neural data of neuroscience. Serving as an interdisciplinary cornerstone, computational neuroscience formalizes the hierarchical and dynamic structures of language into testable neural models through modeling, simulation, and data analysis. This enables a computational dialogue between linguistic hypotheses and neural mechanisms. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly large language models (LLMs), have powerfully advanced this pursuit. Their high-dimensional representational spaces provide a novel scale for exploring the neural basis of linguistic processing, while the "model-brain alignment" framework offers a methodology to evaluate the biological plausibility of language-related theories.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of Morphological Content in BERT Models for Multiple Languages
papers.research_question: To what extent do BERT-style models encode morphological feature information in their hidden representations and attention distributions for multiple languages?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that BERT-style models encode morphological information by partitioning their embedding space into convex regions correlated with feature values, that contextualized embeddings help disambiguate ambiguous forms but not completely, and that specific attention head/layer combinations focus on subject-verb agreement.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that pre-trained BERT-style models are sensitive to morphological information, with strong performance on feature-value classification and certain attention heads learning to focus attention in a manner consistent with morphological agreement.
papers.key_findings:
BERT-style models partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value.
Contextualized embeddings allow models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases.
Specific attention head/layer combinations hone in on subject-verb agreement.
Supervision significantly aids in extracting morphological information, as unsupervised clustering performs near random baselines.
Morphological information is best represented in the middle layers for languages with complex morphology (German and Russian), while for simpler languages it is present throughout all layers.
papers.limitation:
Models have difficulty disambiguating syncretic (ambiguous) forms, especially in languages with complex inflectional morphology.
The classification tasks require supervision; unsupervised methods (k-means) perform near random baselines.
future_direction: Identifying morphological information in BERT-style models in an unsupervised fashion.
Improving models' ability to disambiguate syncretic forms for languages with complex inflectional morphology.
Further exploration of how morphological information is shared between words via self-attention.
papers.abstract: This work describes experiments which probe the hidden representations of several BERT-style models for morphological content. The goal is to examine the extent to which discrete linguistic structure, in the form of morphological features and feature values, presents itself in the vector representations and attention distributions of pre-trained language models for five European languages. The experiments contained herein show that (i) Transformer architectures largely partition their embedding space into convex sub-regions highly correlated with morphological feature value, (ii) the contextualized nature of transformer embeddings allows models to distinguish ambiguous morphological forms in many, but not all cases, and (iii) very specific attention head/layer combinations appear to hone in on subject-verb agreement.

papers.title: Beyond English-Centric LLMs: What Language Do Multilingual Language Models Think in?
papers.research_question: What internal latent language do non-English-centric large language models use in their intermediate layers when processing tasks?
papers.core_contribution: This study demonstrates that the internal latent language of LLMs is determined by their training corpora, with Japanese-specific models using Japanese as a latent language. For non-dominant target languages, models activate the latent language most closely related to it, and the transition from latent to target language occurs in sparse dimensions related to language identity.
papers.conclusion: The internal latent language of LLMs is majorly determined by the language of its training corpora. The transition from latent to target language involves sparse dimensions related to language identity, providing insights for understanding model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Japanese-specific models (Swallow, LLM-jp) use Japanese as an internal latent language when processing Japanese, unlike English-centric Llama-2.
When processing non-dominant languages (French, Chinese), Swallow and LLM-jp exhibit dual internal latent languages (English and Japanese), preferring the one more closely related to the target language.
In culture-conflict QA tasks, intermediate layers initially produce answers biased by the culture of the internal latent language before aligning with the target language context.
The shift from internal latent language to target language representation occurs only in sparse dimensions of the hidden vectors, which are inferred to be related to language identity.
papers.limitation: An exception in Swallow's translation results (higher Japanese probability for French target than Chinese) may be due to specific content in its training corpus, but this hypothesis is difficult to verify.
future_direction: Extend investigation to models with other specific dominant languages, such as Chinese, French, and Arabic.
papers.abstract: In this study, we investigate whether non-English-centric LLMs, despite their strong performance, `think' in their respective dominant language: more precisely, `think' refers to how the representations of intermediate layers, when un-embedded into the vocabulary space, exhibit higher probabilities for certain dominant languages during generation. We term such languages as internal $\textbf{latent languages}$. We examine the latent language of three typical categories of models for Japanese processing: Llama2, an English-centric model; Swallow, an English-centric model with continued pre-training in Japanese; and LLM-jp, a model pre-trained on balanced English and Japanese corpora. Our empirical findings reveal that, unlike Llama2 which relies exclusively on English as the internal latent language, Japanese-specific Swallow and LLM-jp employ both Japanese and English, exhibiting dual internal latent languages. For any given target language, the model preferentially activates the latent language most closely related to it. In addition, we explore how intermediate layers respond to questions involving cultural conflicts between latent internal and target output languages. We further explore how the language identity shifts across layers while keeping consistent semantic meaning reflected in the intermediate layer representations. This study deepens the understanding of non-English-centric large language models, highlighting the intricate dynamics of language representation within their intermediate layers.

papers.title: Echoes of BERT: Do Modern Language Models Rediscover the Classical NLP Pipeline?
papers.research_question: How do modern language models encode linguistic structure, and do they rediscover the classical NLP pipeline observed in earlier models like BERT?
papers.core_contribution: Modern language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline, with lexical information concentrated in early layers and becoming nonlinear, while inflectional morphology remains linearly accessible across layers and languages.
papers.conclusion: Modern transformer language models rediscover the classical NLP pipeline and exhibit robust representational regularities for lexical and inflectional information across architectures, sizes, and languages.
papers.key_findings:
Modern LMs consistently organize linguistic information hierarchically: early layers process syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entities, later layers capture discourse.
Lexical identity (lemma) information is most accessible in early layers and becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network.
Inflectional morphology remains highly linearly accessible across all layers and across six typologically diverse languages.
These representational patterns emerge early during pretraining and are robust across model architectures, sizes, and training regimes.
Inflectional features occupy compact, linearly accessible subspaces in the residual stream, enabling effective steering interventions.
papers.limitation:
Representation extraction for decoder-only models uses the final subword token, which may not be optimal for all architectures.
The study does not explicitly examine cases where different grammatical functions share the same surface form (e.g., infinitive and non-past verb forms).
Classifiers only detect correlations in hidden activations, not causal mechanisms.
Steering experiments measure changes in classifier performance rather than downstream model outputs.
future_direction: Develop better extraction methods for word representations from decoder-only models.
Examine how models separate form from function across languages in cases of surface-form ambiguity.
Design more complex experiments to evaluate steering effects on actual model generation.
papers.abstract: Large transformer-based language models dominate modern NLP, yet our understanding of how they encode linguistic information relies primarily on studies of early models like BERT and GPT-2. Building on classic BERTology work, we analyze 25 models spanning from classical architectures (BERT, DeBERTa, GPT-2) to modern large language models (Pythia, OLMo-2, Gemma-2, Qwen2.5, Llama-3.1), probing layer-by-layer representations across eight linguistic tasks in English. Consistent with earlier findings, we find that hierarchical organization persists in modern models: early layers capture syntax, middle layers handle semantics and entity-level information, and later layers encode discourse phenomena. We dive deeper, conducting an in-depth multilingual analysis of two specific linguistic properties - lexical identity and inflectional morphology - that help disentangle form from meaning. We find that lexical information concentrates linearly in early layers but becomes increasingly nonlinear deeper in the network, while inflectional information remains linearly accessible throughout all layers. Additional analyses of attention mechanisms, steering vectors, and pretraining checkpoints reveal where this information resides within layers, how it can be functionally manipulated, and how representations evolve during pretraining. Taken together, our findings suggest that, even with substantial advances in LLM technologies, transformer models learn to organize linguistic information in similar ways, regardless of model architecture, size, or training regime, indicating that these properties are important for next token prediction. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml5885/model_internal_sleuthing

papers.title: How multilingual is Multilingual BERT?
papers.research_question: Why is Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) effective at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer?
papers.core_contribution: M-BERT learns multilingual representations from monolingual corpora, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, but transfer effectiveness depends on typological similarity and script consistency.
papers.conclusion: M-BERT's cross-lingual transfer ability is due to multilingual representations learned from monolingual data, but for full effectiveness across all language pairs, explicit multilingual training objectives are needed.
papers.key_findings:
M-BERT can perform cross-lingual transfer even between languages with different scripts, indicating deep multilingual representations beyond vocabulary memorization.
Transfer performance is higher for typologically similar languages, suggesting that the model maps structures but does not learn systematic transformations for different word orders.
M-BERT generalizes to code-switched text when trained on monolingual data, showing its multilingual representation capability.
The model struggles with transliterated text, indicating limitations in handling non-standard scripts without explicit training.
The feature space of M-BERT allows for finding translation pairs through vector arithmetic, demonstrating a shared multilingual subspace.
papers.limitation:
Transfer is less accurate for languages with different word orders, such as English and Japanese.
M-BERT does not generalize well to transliterated text without explicit transliteration signals.
future_direction: Incorporate explicit multilingual training objectives to improve transfer to typologically divergent and transliterated targets.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we show that Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), released by Devlin et al. (2018) as a single language model pre-trained from monolingual corpora in 104 languages, is surprisingly good at zero-shot cross-lingual model transfer, in which task-specific annotations in one language are used to fine-tune the model for evaluation in another language. To understand why, we present a large number of probing experiments, showing that transfer is possible even to languages in different scripts, that transfer works best between typologically similar languages, that monolingual corpora can train models for code-switching, and that the model can find translation pairs. From these results, we can conclude that M-BERT does create multilingual representations, but that these representations exhibit systematic deficiencies affecting certain language pairs.

papers.title: Emergence of a High-Dimensional Abstraction Phase in Language Transformers
papers.research_question: What does the evolution of intrinsic dimension (ID) over layers reveal about representational generalizability and linguistic processing in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a distinct high-dimensionality phase in the intermediate layers of language transformers, which corresponds to the first full linguistic abstraction of the input and is predictive of model performance.
papers.conclusion: Different LMs consistently develop a central-layer phase where the intrinsic dimension is expanded, which is the locus of deeper linguistic processing.
papers.key_findings:
A distinct phase characterized by a peak in the intrinsic dimension of representations emerges in intermediate layers across five transformer-based LMs.
This high-ID phase is significantly reduced with random text and absent in untrained models, indicating it reflects learned linguistic structure.
The layer at which the ID peak appears correlates with language modeling quality.
The highest-dimensional representations of different networks predict each other, suggesting they encode similar abstract information.
The ID peak marks a transition from surface-form to syntactic and semantic processing, and representations within it are the first to viably transfer to downstream tasks.
papers.limitation: The paper focuses on detecting broad qualitative patterns; future work should establish a clearer causal connection between intrinsic dimension and language processing via layer ablation studies.
future_direction: Establish causal connection via layer ablations and constraining dimensionality during processing.
Test the effect of pruning inside and outside the ID peak.
Study the relation between the ID profile and specific circuits detected in mechanistic interpretability work.
Use ID profiles for model pruning, fine-tuning, model stitching, and brain encoding models.
papers.abstract: A language model (LM) is a mapping from a linguistic context to an output token. However, much remains to be known about this mapping, including how its geometric properties relate to its function. We take a high-level geometric approach to its analysis, observing, across five pre-trained transformer-based LMs and three input datasets, a distinct phase characterized by high intrinsic dimensionality. During this phase, representations (1) correspond to the first full linguistic abstraction of the input; (2) are the first to viably transfer to downstream tasks; (3) predict each other across different LMs. Moreover, we find that an earlier onset of the phase strongly predicts better language modelling performance. In short, our results suggest that a central high-dimensionality phase underlies core linguistic processing in many common LM architectures.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Open Sesame: Getting inside BERT’s Linguistic Knowledge
papers.research_question: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information?
papers.core_contribution: BERT encodes positional information in lower layers and switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. The paper also introduces a 'confusion score' to quantify intrusion effects in BERT's self-attention mechanism.
papers.conclusion: BERT composes increasingly abstract hierarchical representations of linguistic structure using self-attention, but does not show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure found in human processing.
papers.key_findings:
Diagnostic classifiers show BERT's lower layers encode positional information well, while higher layers encode hierarchical information.
The proposed confusion score reveals BERT's attention is sensitive to syntactic structure and grammatical features (number, gender) in subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora.
BERT's attention is not perfectly syntactic; it sometimes attends to grammatically inaccessible or mismatched distractors.
Confusion scores decrease with layer depth, and there is an increase in confusion at layer 4, coinciding with the degradation of positional information.
BERT's performance on possessive constructions in the subject noun task is poor, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
papers.limitation:
BERT performed poorly on possessive constructions in the subject noun task, possibly due to ambiguity of the 's token.
BERT's attention is only incompletely modulated by structural and featural properties, and attention is sometimes spread across grammatically irrelevant elements.
future_direction: Investigate or visualize layer-on-layer changes in BERT’s structural and positional information, particularly between layers 3 and 4.
Retrieve the increasingly hierarchical representations of BERT across layers via the self-attention mechanism.
papers.abstract: How and to what extent does BERT encode syntactically-sensitive hierarchical information or positionally-sensitive linear information? Recent work has shown that contextual representations like BERT perform well on tasks that require sensitivity to linguistic structure. We present here two studies which aim to provide a better understanding of the nature of BERT's representations. The first of these focuses on the identification of structurally-defined elements using diagnostic classifiers, while the second explores BERT's representation of subject-verb agreement and anaphor-antecedent dependencies through a quantitative assessment of self-attention vectors. In both cases, we find that BERT encodes positional information about word tokens well on its lower layers, but switches to a hierarchically-oriented encoding on higher layers. We conclude then that BERT's representations do indeed model linguistically relevant aspects of hierarchical structure, though they do not appear to show the sharp sensitivity to hierarchical structure that is found in human processing of reflexive anaphora.

papers.title: Identifying and Controlling Important Neurons in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: How important are individual neurons for obtaining high-quality translations? Do individual neurons in NMT models contain interpretable linguistic information? Can we control MT output by intervening in the representation at the individual neuron level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper develops unsupervised methods (based on correlations between models) for discovering important neurons in Neural Machine Translation models, shows these neurons impact translation quality and capture linguistic phenomena, and demonstrates how to control translations by modifying their activations.
papers.conclusion: The work indicates that not all information is distributed in NMT models, and that many human-interpretable grammatical and structural properties are captured by individual neurons. Moreover, modifying the activations of individual neurons allows controlling the translation output according to specified linguistic properties.
papers.key_findings:
Unsupervised correlation methods (MaxCorr, MinCorr, LinReg, SVCCA) can rank neurons by importance, with top-ranked neurons having a larger impact on translation quality when erased.
Many top-ranked neurons capture interpretable linguistic properties such as position in sentence, parentheses, tense, number, gender, and noun phrase segmentation.
Modifying the activations of individual neurons (e.g., tense neurons) allows for controlling translation output (e.g., changing verb tense) with varying degrees of success.
Different ranking methods highlight different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find information distributed across tokens.
The work indicates that not all linguistic information in NMT models is fully distributed; some properties are captured by individual neurons.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional seq2seq).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Apply the methods to other tasks beyond machine translation.
papers.abstract:
Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing
substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such
information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to
individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important
neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models
learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision.
We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered
neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena.
Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by
modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Exploring Concept Depth: How Large Language Models Acquire Knowledge and Concept at Different Layers?
papers.research_question: Can shallow layers in LLMs capture meaningful features of simple knowledge, while complex concepts need deeper layers to capture their meaningful features?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the concept of 'Concept Depth' to measure how different layers in LLMs capture concepts of varying complexity, showing that simpler concepts are learned in shallow layers while complex concepts require deeper layers.
papers.conclusion: The Concept Depth metric provides a useful framework for understanding how LLMs process concepts of varying complexity across layers, and the experimental insights enhance the understanding of internal representations in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Simpler concepts (e.g., factual knowledge) are learned in shallow layers, while more complex concepts (e.g., reasoning tasks) require deeper layers for accurate understanding.
The pattern of Concept Depth is consistent across different model families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) and model sizes.
Larger models within a family tend to achieve higher peak accuracy and sometimes converge to optimal performance at earlier layers.
Adding noise to the input or quantizing model weights (e.g., to 8-bit) slows down the convergence of concept understanding, requiring deeper layers to achieve comparable accuracy.
Compressing models to 16-bit quantization does not significantly harm the understanding process compared to 32-bit.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable performances across a wide range of tasks. However, the mechanisms by which these models encode tasks of varying complexities remain poorly understood. In this paper, we explore the hypothesis that LLMs process concepts of varying complexities in different layers, introducing the idea of "Concept Depth" to suggest that more complex concepts are typically acquired in deeper layers. Specifically, we categorize concepts based on their level of abstraction, defining them in the order of increasing complexity within factual, emotional, and inferential tasks. We conduct extensive probing experiments using layer-wise representations across various LLM families (Gemma, LLaMA, Qwen) on various datasets spanning the three domains of tasks. Our findings reveal that models could efficiently conduct probing for simpler tasks in shallow layers, and more complex tasks typically necessitate deeper layers for accurate understanding. Additionally, we examine how external factors, such as adding noise to the input and quantizing the model weights, might affect layer-wise representations. Our findings suggest that these factors can impede the development of a conceptual understanding of LLMs until deeper layers are explored. We hope that our proposed concept and experimental insights will enhance the understanding of the mechanisms underlying LLMs. Our codes are available at https://github.com/Luckfort/CD.

papers.title: More than Correlation: Do Large Language Models Learn Causal Representations of Space?
papers.research_question: Does the internal spatial representation in large language models have a causal effect on their behavior in geospatial tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models learn internal spatial representations of location words, and these representations causally influence the model's performance on geospatial tasks.
papers.conclusion: Through representational similarity analysis and probing, the paper shows that both DeBERTa-v2 and GPT-Neo learned spatial representations of location words, and intervention experiments demonstrate these representations have causal effects on model output.
papers.key_findings:
The hidden states of city names in DeBERTa and GPT-Neo correlate with real-world geospatial distances, as shown by representational similarity analysis.
Linear and non-linear probes can map hidden states to latitude and longitude with low error, indicating the presence of spatial information.
A novel GeoDist loss function, which accounts for spherical geometry, improves probing performance over mean squared error.
Causal intervention experiments show that aligning hidden states with true geographic coordinates improves accuracy in a country prediction task, while misaligning degrades it.
Perturbing hidden states with spatial information affects next-word prediction for country names, demonstrating causal use of spatial representations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to location words and geospatial tasks; it is unclear how spatial representations affect other types of words and non-geospatial tasks.
future_direction: Investigate spatial representations for words without inherent geographical property
Study the effect of spatial representation perturbation on tasks that do not rely on geographical knowledge
papers.abstract: Recent work found high mutual information between the learned representations of large language models (LLMs) and the geospatial property of its input, hinting an emergent internal model of space. However, whether this internal space model has any causal effects on the LLMs' behaviors was not answered by that work, led to criticism of these findings as mere statistical correlation. Our study focused on uncovering the causality of the spatial representations in LLMs. In particular, we discovered the potential spatial representations in DeBERTa, GPT-Neo using representational similarity analysis and linear and non-linear probing. Our casual intervention experiments showed that the spatial representations influenced the model's performance on next word prediction and a downstream task that relies on geospatial information. Our experiments suggested that the LLMs learn and use an internal model of space in solving geospatial related tasks.

papers.title: SVCCA: Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis for Deep Learning Dynamics and Interpretability
papers.research_question: What is the intrinsic dimensionality of layers in neural networks and how do learning dynamics evolve during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SVCCA, a method for comparing neural network representations, and uses it to show that layers are over-parameterized, learning converges from bottom up, and proposes Freeze Training to save computation and improve generalization.
papers.conclusion: SVCCA is a powerful tool for comparing learned representations across layers, architectures, and time, providing insights into learning dynamics and motivating new training and compression techniques.
papers.key_findings:
The intrinsic dimensionality of a layer is often much smaller than the number of neurons, indicating over-parameterization.
Learning dynamics show that networks converge from the bottom up, with lower layers solidifying before higher ones.
SVCCA can capture semantic similarities between classes, with similar classes having similar sensitivity patterns in the network.
Freeze Training, which sequentially freezes lower layers during training, can save computation and sometimes improve generalization.
The important directions found by SVCCA are distributed across many neurons rather than being axis-aligned.
papers.abstract: We propose a new technique, Singular Vector Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA), a tool for quickly comparing two representations in a way that is both invariant to affine transform (allowing comparison between different layers and networks) and fast to compute (allowing more comparisons to be calculated than with previous methods). We deploy this tool to measure the intrinsic dimensionality of layers, showing in some cases needless over-parameterization; to probe learning dynamics throughout training, finding that networks converge to final representations from the bottom up; to show where class-specific information in networks is formed; and to suggest new training regimes that simultaneously save computation and overfit less. Code: https://github.com/google/svcca/

papers.title: The Bottom-up Evolution of Representations in the Transformer: A Study with Machine Translation and Language Modeling Objectives
papers.research_question: How do the representations of individual tokens and the structure of the learned feature space evolve between layers in Transformers under different learning objectives (machine translation, language modeling, masked language modeling)?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes viewing token representation evolution in Transformers through a compression/prediction trade-off, and shows through experiments that different objectives (MT, LM, MLM) lead to distinct patterns of information flow, with MLM exhibiting a two-stage process of context encoding and token reconstruction.
papers.conclusion: The learning objective determines the information flow in the model, and the proposed compression/prediction perspective helps explain the behavior and relates findings to prior probing task results, suggesting MLM may be superior for pretraining.
papers.key_findings:
For LM, as you go from bottom to top layers, information about the past gets lost and predictions about the future get formed.
