Different ranking methods capture different types of information: MaxCorr and MinCorr tend to find position information, while LinReg and SVCCA find token identity information.
The methods are task-independent and can be applied to other neural networks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is applied only to LSTM-based NMT models; application to other architectures like the Transformer is left for future work.
Controlling some properties (e.g., gender) is more difficult, possibly because they are more distributed than others (e.g., tense).
future_direction: Apply the analysis to other NMT components (e.g., the decoder) and architectures (e.g., Transformer, convolutional sequence-to-sequence).
Develop more sophisticated ways to control translation output, for example by modifying representations in variational NMT architectures.
Analyze the spectrum of localized vs. distributed information in neural language representations more broadly.
papers.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) models learn representations containing substantial linguistic information. However, it is not clear if such information is fully distributed or if some of it can be attributed to individual neurons. We develop unsupervised methods for discovering important neurons in NMT models. Our methods rely on the intuition that different models learn similar properties, and do not require any costly external supervision. We show experimentally that translation quality depends on the discovered neurons, and find that many of them capture common linguistic phenomena. Finally, we show how to control NMT translations in predictable ways, by modifying activations of individual neurons.

papers.title: Large Language Models are Locally Linear Mappings
papers.research_question: How can we map LLM inference for a given input sequence to an equivalent and interpretable linear system that reconstructs the predicted output embedding with high precision, without requiring additional model training?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a method to compute an equivalent linear system for a given input sequence to a transformer decoder LLM, which reconstructs the predicted output embedding with relative error below 1e-13 at double floating-point precision, requiring no additional model training.
papers.conclusion: Despite their expressive power and global nonlinearity, modern LLMs can be interpreted through equivalent linear representations that reveal low-dimensional semantic structures in the next-token prediction process.
papers.key_findings:
The detached Jacobian method can reconstruct the output embedding of LLMs with high precision (relative error <1e-13).
The equivalent linear system is very low-rank, indicating that the model operates in low-dimensional subspaces.
The singular vectors of the detached Jacobian can be decoded to interpretable semantic concepts.
The method can be applied layer-wise and to individual attention and MLP modules, showing how predictions are built.
The detached Jacobian can be used as a steering operator to insert semantic concepts into unrelated text.
papers.limitation: The method is local (pointwise) and must be recomputed for each input sequence; it is not piecewise linear and does not generalize to local neighborhoods.
future_direction: Explore scaling the method to many token predictions and analyzing the linear systems across diverse contexts, tasks, domains, and model architectures.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate that the inference operations of several open-weight large language models (LLMs) can be mapped to an exactly equivalent linear system for an input sequence without modifying the model weights or altering output predictions. Extending techniques from image diffusion models that exhibit local or piecewise linearity, we strategically alter the gradient computation with respect to a given input sequence for a next-token prediction such that the Jacobian of the model nearly exactly reproduces the forward prediction with a linear system. We demonstrate this approach across models (Llama 3, Gemma 3, Qwen 3, Phi 4, Mistral Ministral and OLMo 2, up to Llama 3.3 70B Q4) and show through the singular value decomposition of the detached Jacobian that these LLMs operate in extremely low-dimensional subspaces where many of the largest singular vectors decode to concepts related to the most-likely output token. This approach also allows us to examine the operation of each successive layer (and its attention and MLP components) as nearly-exact linear systems and observe the emergence of semantic concepts. Despite their expressive power and global nonlinearity, modern LLMs can be interpreted through nearly-exact locally linear decompositions that provide insights into their internal representations and reveal interpretable semantic structures in the next-token prediction process.

papers.title: Same Neurons, Different Languages: Probing Morphosyntax in Multilingual Pre-trained Models
papers.research_question: Do multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in the same subset of neurons across different languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual pre-trained models encode morphosyntactic information in overlapping subsets of neurons across languages, with the extent of overlap varying by category, language proximity, and pre-training data size.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual pre-trained models develop cross-lingually entangled representations of morphosyntax, which may underpin their ability to generalize across languages and facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
There is significant cross-lingual overlap of neurons encoding morphosyntactic information.
The overlap varies across morphosyntactic categories and tends to be lower for categories with larger inventories of possible values.
Neuron subsets are shared more between languages in the same genus or with similar typological features.
Overlap increases with the amount of pre-training data for a language.
Overlap decreases in larger model architectures (comparing XLM-R-base and XLM-R-large).
future_direction: Artificially encouraging tighter neuron overlap might facilitate zero-shot cross-lingual inference to low-resource and typologically distant languages.
papers.abstract: Karolina Stanczak, Edoardo Ponti, Lucas Torroba Hennigen, Ryan Cotterell, Isabelle Augenstein. Proceedings of the 2022 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies. 2022.

papers.title: Understanding trained CNNs by indexing neuron selectivity
papers.research_question: How can we understand and visualize the internal representations of Convolutional Neural Networks by indexing neuron selectivity to specific properties like color and class?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework to understand CNN internal representations by visualizing Neuron Features and quantifying neuron selectivity indexes for color and class, enabling the analysis of how features and classes are represented across layers.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully indexes neuron selectivity, showing how color and class representations are organized across CNN layers, with implications for understanding neural coding principles.
papers.key_findings:
Color selectivity is present in all convolutional layers, with 40% in conv1 and 30% in conv2, decreasing but still present in deeper layers.
Class selectivity increases with depth, with over 50% of neurons in conv5 having high class selectivity (index >0.6).
Neuron Feature visualization reveals clear shapes for some neurons and blurred features for others, suggesting different coding strategies.
The framework can identify specific neurons selective to colors or classes, such as a red-mushroom neuron in conv4 or dog-face neurons in conv5.
Color is important for object recognition, as grayscale images lead to higher classification errors.
future_direction: Apply indexes to different neural network architectures.
Define new selectivity indexes for shape, texture, or part detection.
Study relations between indexes.

papers.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
papers.research_question: How do neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules, specifically in the context of cellular automata?
papers.core_contribution: Shows that convolutional neural networks can represent and learn arbitrary cellular automata rules, and that the internal representations of trained networks reflect the complexity (entropy) of the CA rules.
papers.conclusion: Convolutional neural networks can learn cellular automata rules, and the complexity of the rules affects the depth and specialization of the learned representations, suggesting that the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Any cellular automaton can be represented by a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture.
A general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture can learn arbitrary CA rules when given videos of the CA as training data.
In the limit of large network widths, training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates.
Cellular automata with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations.
The entropy of the CA rule table influences the specificity of the internal representations in the trained network.
future_direction: Determine whether neural networks can more broadly inform efforts to understand the dynamical space of CA, including relating a CA's a priori rules to its apparent dynamical complexity during simulation.
Relate observations to more general patterns in deep networks, such as the information bottleneck.
papers.abstract: Deep-learning techniques have recently demonstrated broad success in predicting complex dynamical systems ranging from turbulence to human speech, motivating broader questions about how neural networks encode and represent dynamical rules. We explore this problem in the context of cellular automata (CA), simple dynamical systems that are intrinsically discrete and thus difficult to analyze using standard tools from dynamical systems theory. We show that any CA may readily be represented using a convolutional neural network with a network-in-network architecture. This motivates the development of a general convolutional multilayer perceptron architecture, which we find can learn the dynamical rules for arbitrary CA when given videos of the CA as training data. In the limit of large network widths, we find that training dynamics are nearly identical across replicates, and that common patterns emerge in the structure of networks trained on different CA rulesets. We train ensembles of networks on randomly sampled CA, and we probe how the trained networks internally represent the CA rules using an information-theoretic technique based on distributions of layer activation patterns. We find that CA with simpler rule tables produce trained networks with hierarchical structure and layer specialization, while more complex CA produce shallower representations-illustrating how the underlying complexity of the CA's rules influences the specificity of these internal representations. Our results suggest how the entropy of a physical process can affect its representation when learned by neural networks.

papers.title: Probing for the Usage of Grammatical Number
papers.research_question: How does BERT encode grammatical number, and does it actually use that encoding when solving the number agreement task?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a usage-based probing setup to find functional encodings, and shows that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number for number agreement, with separate encodings for nouns and verbs, and identifies transfer layers.
papers.conclusion: The usage-based probing method allows tracking how grammatical number is encoded and transferred in BERT, showing that interventions impact behavior and extractability, revealing orthogonal encodings for nouns and verbs, and indirect transfer through intermediate tokens.
papers.key_findings:
BERT relies on a linear functional encoding of grammatical number to solve the number agreement task.
BERT uses separate encodings of grammatical number for nouns and verbs.
Number information is transferred from noun to verb between layers 3 and 8.
The transfer occurs indirectly through intermediate tokens, not directly via attention.
The encoding found by diagnostic probes is actually used by the model (functional).
papers.limitation:
The dataset may not be fully representative of the number agreement task.
Amnesic probing may remove more information than necessary.
papers.abstract: A central quest of probing is to uncover how pre-trained models encode a linguistic property within their representations. An encoding, however, might be spurious-i.e., the model might not rely on it when making predictions. In this paper, we try to find an encoding that the model actually uses, introducing a usage-based probing setup. We first choose a behavioral task which cannot be solved without using the linguistic property. Then, we attempt to remove the property by intervening on the model's representations. We contend that, if an encoding is used by the model, its removal should harm the performance on the chosen behavioral task. As a case study, we focus on how BERT encodes grammatical number, and on how it uses this encoding to solve the number agreement task. Experimentally, we find that BERT relies on a linear encoding of grammatical number to produce the correct behavioral output. We also find that BERT uses a separate encoding of grammatical number for nouns and verbs. Finally, we identify in which layers information about grammatical number is transferred from a noun to its head verb.

papers.title: Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models
papers.research_question: What is the nature of feature representations in sequence models? Specifically, are world models linearly encoded in the activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The board state in OthelloGPT is linearly encoded relative to the current player (MINE vs. YOURS), enabling control of the model's behavior via simple vector arithmetic.
papers.conclusion: The emergent world model in OthelloGPT is linearly represented, enabling interpretability and control via vector arithmetic, and revealing multiple circuits and iterative refinement across layers.
papers.key_findings:
OthelloGPT linearly encodes the board state relative to the current player (MINE/YOURS) rather than absolute colors, achieving high accuracy with linear probes.
Simple vector addition of linear directions (MINE, YOURS, EMPTY) to the residual stream can causally alter the model's believed board state and move predictions.
The model also linearly encodes which tiles are flipped at each timestep, as shown by high F1 scores with linear probes.
Evidence suggests multiple circuits exist: in end games, legal moves are sometimes computed before the full board state is accurately represented.
The model iteratively refines board state and move predictions across layers, with accuracy improving layer by layer.
papers.limitation:
Probing requires knowing which features to look for, and human preconceptions may lead to incorrect interpretations.
The model's board state accuracy drops in end games, and it may use alternative circuits, indicating incomplete understanding.
future_direction: Investigate why linear feature representations emerge and what linear representations exist in large language models.
papers.abstract: How do sequence models represent their decision-making process? Prior work suggests that Othello-playing neural network learned nonlinear models of the board state (Li et al., 2023a). In this work, we provide evidence of a closely related linear representation of the board. In particular, we show that probing for "my colour" vs. "opponent's colour" may be a simple yet powerful way to interpret the model's internal state. This precise understanding of the internal representations allows us to control the model's behaviour with simple vector arithmetic. Linear representations enable significant interpretability progress, which we demonstrate with further exploration of how the world model is computed.

papers.title: Sharing Matters: Analysing Neurons Across Languages and Tasks in LLMs
papers.research_question: How is neuron activation shared across tasks and languages in multilingual large language models (LLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a fine-grained neuron classification method for multilingual LLMs and demonstrates that neurons shared across all languages (all-shared neurons) are crucial for model performance and generating accurate responses.
papers.conclusion: The study improves understanding of the internal workings of multilingual LLMs by showing the pivotal role of cross-lingually shared neurons and the task- and model-dependent nature of neuron activation patterns, paving the way for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Deactivating all-shared neurons significantly decreases model performance across tasks (up to 87.39% drop in accuracy).
All-shared neurons have the greatest impact on generating both answers and correct answers, as measured by Generation Impact Score and Correctness Impact Score.
Neuron activation patterns vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages; for example, instruction-finetuned models show more all-shared neurons than foundation models.
Neuron sharing does not always align with language similarity; languages from the same family do not necessarily share more neurons.
Deactivating certain neuron types (partial-shared or specific) can occasionally improve performance for some languages, possibly due to mitigating knowledge conflicts.
future_direction: More in-depth investigation of how factual knowledge is stored and shared across languages in LLMs.
Further exploration of the relationship between language similarity and neuron sharing.
Investigation of whether in-context learning leads to better neuron activation composition rather than invoking more neurons.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have revolutionized the field of natural language processing (NLP), and recent studies have aimed to understand their underlying mechanisms. However, most of this research is conducted within a monolingual setting, primarily focusing on English. Few studies have attempted to explore the internal workings of LLMs in multilingual settings. In this study, we aim to fill this research gap by examining how neuron activation is shared across tasks and languages. We classify neurons into four distinct categories based on their responses to a specific input across different languages: all-shared, partial-shared, specific, and non-activated. Building upon this categorisation, we conduct extensive experiments on three tasks across nine languages using several LLMs and present an in-depth analysis in this work. Our findings reveal that: (i) deactivating the all-shared neurons significantly decreases performance; (ii) the shared neurons play a vital role in generating responses, especially for the all-shared neurons; (iii) neuron activation patterns are highly sensitive and vary across tasks, LLMs, and languages. These findings shed light on the internal workings of multilingual LLMs and pave the way for future research. We release the code to foster research in this area.

papers.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
papers.research_question: How are model predictions refined layer by layer in transformers through iterative inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the tuned lens, a method that trains affine probes to decode hidden states in frozen pretrained transformers, providing more reliable and unbiased prediction trajectories than the logit lens.
papers.conclusion: The tuned lens is a drop-in replacement for the logit lens that provides interpretable prediction trajectories and has applications in anomaly detection and difficulty estimation.
papers.key_findings:
The tuned lens produces lower perplexity and less biased predictions than the logit lens across various models.
Causal experiments show that features influential on the tuned lens are also causally relevant to the model's output.
The tuned lens can detect prompt injection attacks with near-perfect accuracy in some cases.
Prediction depth from the tuned lens correlates with the iteration learned during training, indicating it measures example difficulty.
Tuned lens translators transfer well to fine-tuned models without additional training.
papers.limitation:
Training translators for each layer requires additional computation compared to the logit lens.
Causal basis extraction is computationally intensive.
future_direction: Make causal basis extraction more scalable.
Apply the tuned lens to other modalities beyond language.
papers.abstract: We analyze transformers from the perspective of iterative inference, seeking to understand how model predictions are refined layer by layer. To do so, we train an affine probe for each block in a frozen pretrained model, making it possible to decode every hidden state into a distribution over the vocabulary. Our method, the tuned lens, is a refinement of the earlier "logit lens" technique, which yielded useful insights but is often brittle. We test our method on various autoregressive language models with up to 20B parameters, showing it to be more predictive, reliable and unbiased than the logit lens. With causal experiments, we show the tuned lens uses similar features to the model itself. We also find the trajectory of latent predictions can be used to detect malicious inputs with high accuracy. All code needed to reproduce our results can be found at https://github.com/AlignmentResearch/tuned-lens.

papers.title: Analytical and numerical study of internal representations in multilayer neural networks with binary weights
papers.research_question: The paper investigates the weight space structure of multilayer neural networks with binary weights, focusing on the distribution of volumes associated with internal representations of learning examples. It also analyzes the learning behavior and symmetry breaking transition in such networks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies the internal representation volumes approach to multilayer neural networks with binary weights, deriving the distribution of volumes and analyzing learning behavior and symmetry breaking transitions, with numerical validation.
papers.conclusion: The internal representation volumes approach is confirmed by numerical simulations for binary weight networks, revealing differences from continuous weight networks in where symmetry breaking occurs.
papers.key_findings:
The distribution of internal representation volumes for the binary parity machine can be computed analytically, revealing a freezing transition at α=0.41.
The number of implementable internal representations NR and the number of domains contributing to the Gardner volume ND are derived as functions of the loading parameter α.
The analytical predictions show remarkable agreement with numerical simulations on finite systems.
Multilayer networks with binary weights exhibit symmetry breaking inside representation volumes, unlike continuous weights where it occurs between volumes.
The method provides a detailed geometrical interpretation of the learning transition and the freezing phenomena.
future_direction: Study of the distribution of metastable states arising from a gradient learning process.
papers.abstract: We study the weight space structure of the parity machine with binary weights by deriving the distribution of volumes associated to the internal representations of the learning examples. The learning behavior and the symmetry breaking transition are analyzed and the results are found to be in very good agreement with the extended numerical simulations. \textcopyright{} 1996 The American Physical Society.

papers.title: RECALL: REpresentation-aligned Catastrophic-forgetting ALLeviation via Hierarchical Model Merging
papers.research_question: How can we mitigate catastrophic forgetting in large language models without access to historical data, by leveraging internal representations for model merging?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes RECALL, a representation-aware model merging framework that uses layer-wise hidden representation similarities to align and merge models, mitigating catastrophic forgetting without needing historical data.
papers.conclusion: RECALL provides an effective, data-free solution for continual learning in LLMs by aligning representations during model merging, mitigating catastrophic forgetting and enabling multi-domain knowledge fusion.
papers.key_findings:
RECALL outperforms baselines in knowledge retention and generalization across five NLP tasks.
RECALL effectively fuses knowledge from multiple fine-tuned models without access to historical data.
RECALL maintains stable performance in sequential fine-tuning, showing strong resistance to catastrophic forgetting.
Representation similarity (using RBF kernel) is an effective guide for layer-wise model merging.
RECALL works with both single and multiple model merging, and with or without the base model.
papers.limitation:
Assumes access to multiple fine-tuned models on related tasks, which may not always be available.
Relies on clustering and similarity computations over a small set of representative samples, which can influence merging outcome.
Tailored to models with identical architectures and aligned tokenizers; extending to heterogeneous models or multilingual settings is challenging.
Scaling to dozens of tasks or integrating with training-time regularization techniques needs further investigation.
future_direction: Extending RECALL to heterogeneous model families or multilingual settings.
Scaling RECALL to dozens of tasks.
Integrating RECALL with training-time regularization techniques for tighter lifelong learning integration.
papers.abstract: We unveil that internal representations in large language models (LLMs) serve as reliable proxies of learned knowledge, and propose RECALL, a novel representation-aware model merging framework for continual learning without access to historical data. RECALL computes inter-model similarity from layer-wise hidden representations over clustered typical samples, and performs adaptive, hierarchical parameter fusion to align knowledge across models. This design enables the preservation of domain-general features in shallow layers while allowing task-specific adaptation in deeper layers. Unlike prior methods that require task labels or incur performance trade-offs, RECALL achieves seamless multi-domain integration and strong resistance to catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments across five NLP tasks and multiple continual learning scenarios show that RECALL outperforms baselines in both knowledge retention and generalization, providing a scalable and data-free solution for evolving LLMs.

papers.title: Language Models Learn POS First
papers.research_question: How and when are linguistic structures, such as part-of-speech tagging and global topic information, acquired during the training of language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that during training, language models acquire part-of-speech tagging early and global topic information continuously, using methods like gradient concentration and SVCCA.
papers.conclusion: Early training focuses on learning part-of-speech syntax for initial performance, while later training shifts to refining global topic representations for further gains.
papers.key_findings:
Frequent words have more concentrated gradients, and concentration increases over time during training.
Closed POS classes (e.g., pronouns, prepositions) show early concentration stabilization, while open classes (e.g., nouns, verbs) continue to become more concentrated.
Part-of-speech tagging is learned early in training, with representation peaking before the first optimizer step size rescale.
Global topic information is learned continuously throughout training, with representation increasing over time.
future_direction: Develop ways of interpreting syntactic structures during training.
papers.abstract: A glut of recent research shows that language models capture linguistic structure. Such work answers the question of whether a model represents linguistic structure. But how and when are these structures acquired? Rather than treating the training process itself as a black box, we investigate how representations of linguistic structure are learned over time. In particular, we demonstrate that different aspects of linguistic structure are learned at different rates, with part of speech tagging acquired early and global topic information learned continuously.

papers.title: Predictive Coding or Just Feature Discovery? An Alternative Account of Why Language Models Fit Brain Data
papers.research_question: How related are the representations learned by neural language models, translation models, and language tagging tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to embed language representations into a low-dimensional space based on transferability, and shows that this embedding captures the hierarchical organization of language processing in the human brain.
papers.conclusion: The low-dimensional structure of language representations reflects the structure of language representations in the human brain, and the method provides a template for investigating relationships between linguistic and cognitive representations.
papers.key_findings:
The representation embedding matrix reveals a low-dimensional structure where language models and translation models interpolate between word embeddings, syntactic/semantic tasks, and future word embeddings.
The first dimension of this structure corresponds to a hierarchy from low-level to high-level language processing.
This first dimension maps onto the brain's language processing hierarchy, with early auditory areas explained by lower-level features and higher-order areas by later model layers.
The representation embeddings can predict which representations best explain brain activity in different regions.
Most pairs of representations are discriminable based on their brain activity patterns, indicating the embeddings capture brain representation structure.
papers.limitation:
The chosen set of representations may not capture the full diversity of the space.
The use of GloVe as the universal input representation may not be truly universal.
The use of linear networks may underestimate relatedness between tasks.
future_direction: Using an even larger number of representations to better map the space.
Using other universal spaces, such as directly using fMRI data as input.
Exploring regularized nonlinear models for the encoder-decoder networks.
papers.abstract: Many recent studies have shown that representations drawn from neural network language models are extremely effective at predicting brain responses to natural language. But why do these models work so well? One proposed explanation is that language models and brains are similar because they have the same objective: to predict upcoming words before they are perceived. This explanation is attractive because it lends support to the popular theory of predictive coding. We provide several analyses that cast doubt on this claim. First, we show that the ability to predict future words does not uniquely (or even best) explain why some representations are a better match to the brain than others. Second, we show that within a language model, representations that are best at predicting future words are strictly worse brain models than other representations. Finally, we argue in favor of an alternative explanation for the success of language models in neuroscience: These models are effective at predicting brain responses because they generally capture a wide variety of linguistic phenomena.

papers.title: Natural language instructions induce compositional generalization in networks of neurons
papers.research_question: What neural computations allow networks to interpret linguistic instructions and perform novel tasks without explicit experience?
papers.core_contribution: Language instructions enable zero-shot generalization in neural networks by aligning sensorimotor representations with the semantic geometry of instructions, allowing composition of practiced skills for novel tasks.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how linguistic instructions induce compositional generalization in neural networks, offering testable predictions for neural representations underlying flexible cognition in the human brain.
papers.key_findings:
Models using sentence-level semantics (e.g., SBERT) achieve up to 83% correct zero-shot generalization on unseen tasks.
Language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that their geometry shares structure with instruction embeddings, facilitating compositionality.
Individual neurons in the sensorimotor network modulate their tuning based on the semantics of instructions.
The network can produce linguistic descriptions of novel tasks based solely on motor feedback, enabling knowledge transfer to partner models.
Generalization is supported by cross-condition generalization performance (CCGP) metrics that correlate with task performance.
future_direction: Guiding imaging studies to delineate brain areas involved in instruction following
Comparing compositional representations in nonlinguistic subjects like nonhuman primates
papers.abstract: A fundamental human cognitive feat is to interpret linguistic instructions in order to perform novel tasks without explicit task experience. Yet, the neural computations that might be used to accomplish this remain poorly understood. We use advances in natural language processing to create a neural model of generalization based on linguistic instructions. Models are trained on a set of common psychophysical tasks, and receive instructions embedded by a pretrained language model. Our best models can perform a previously unseen task with an average performance of 83% correct based solely on linguistic instructions (that is, zero-shot learning). We found that language scaffolds sensorimotor representations such that activity for interrelated tasks shares a common geometry with the semantic representations of instructions, allowing language to cue the proper composition of practiced skills in unseen settings. We show how this model generates a linguistic description of a novel task it has identified using only motor feedback, which can subsequently guide a partner model to perform the task. Our models offer several experimentally testable predictions outlining how linguistic information must be represented to facilitate flexible and general cognition in the human brain.

papers.title: From Monolingual to Bilingual: Investigating Language Conditioning in Large Language Models for Psycholinguistic Tasks
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages, and how does language identity (monolingual vs bilingual prompting) affect their output behavior and internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that large language models condition their psycholinguistic behavior and internal representations on the language identity specified in the prompt, with differences between monolingual and bilingual prompting, offering insights into cross-linguistic cognition in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results demonstrate that LLMs are not language-neutral. Instead, they respond to and encode language-specific cues in both their outputs and internal representations.
papers.key_findings:
Both models adapt their outputs based on the linguistic identity embedded in the prompt.
Qwen shows greater sensitivity to prompt language and sharper behavioral distinctions between Dutch and Chinese than Llama.
Probing reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more linearly decodable in deeper layers.
Chinese prompts yield stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch prompts.
Bilingual prompting can introduce interference or noise, especially for low-resource languages like Dutch.
papers.limitation:
Focus on only three languages (English, Dutch, Chinese), limiting generalizability.
Only two LLMs are evaluated.
Tasks represent only a narrow slice of the psycholinguistic space.
future_direction: Expanding to include languages with different scripts, phonological systems, or morphological complexity (e.g., Arabic, Hindi, Finnish).
Incorporating a broader set of psycholinguistic phenomena, such as lexical decision making, semantic priming, syntactic ambiguity resolution, and metaphor comprehension.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong linguistic capabilities, but little is known about how they encode psycholinguistic knowledge across languages. We investigate whether and how LLMs exhibit human-like psycholinguistic responses under different linguistic identities using two tasks: sound symbolism and word valence. We evaluate two models, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, under monolingual and bilingual prompting in English, Dutch, and Chinese. Behaviorally, both models adjust their outputs based on prompted language identity, with Qwen showing greater sensitivity and sharper distinctions between Dutch and Chinese. Probing analysis reveals that psycholinguistic signals become more decodable in deeper layers, with Chinese prompts yielding stronger and more stable valence representations than Dutch. Our results demonstrate that language identity conditions both output behavior and internal representations in LLMs, providing new insights into their application as models of cross-linguistic cognition.

papers.title: The Other Mind: How Language Models Exhibit Human Temporal Cognition
papers.research_question: How do large language models exhibit human-like temporal cognition, specifically whether they spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law?
papers.core_contribution: Larger LLMs spontaneously exhibit human-like temporal cognition, establishing a subjective reference point and adhering to the Weber-Fechner law, which emerges from multi-level convergence at neuronal, representational, and informational levels.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit human-like temporal cognition through multi-level convergence, suggesting cognition is a subjective construction of the external world. This points to the risk of alien cognitive frameworks and the need for AI alignment paradigms that guide internal world-building.
papers.key_findings:
In similarity judgment tasks, larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point (ca. 2025) and their perception of time logarithmically compresses as years recede from this point, adhering to the Weber-Fechner law.
A subgroup of temporal-preferential neurons in the FFN exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme similar to biological systems.
Representations of years undergo hierarchical construction: from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation organized around a reference point in deep layers.
Pre-trained embedding models reveal that the training corpus possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, providing raw material for the model's internal construction of temporal cognition.
The findings support an experientialist perspective where LLM cognition is a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system, leading to potential convergence with or divergence from human cognition.
future_direction: Evolve AI alignment beyond behavioral control to a paradigm that actively guides the formation of a model's internal world from its source.
Monitor models' emergent representational and cognitive patterns and enable intervention across the chain of cognition.
Curate the AI's environment with harmless or formalized verifiable information exposures.
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance, they exhibit certain cognitive patterns similar to those of humans that are not directly specified in training data. This study investigates this phenomenon by focusing on temporal cognition in LLMs. Leveraging the similarity judgment task, we find that larger models spontaneously establish a subjective temporal reference point and adhere to the Weber-Fechner law, whereby the perceived distance logarithmically compresses as years recede from this reference point. To uncover the mechanisms behind this behavior, we conducted multiple analyses across neuronal, representational, and informational levels. We first identify a set of temporal-preferential neurons and find that this group exhibits minimal activation at the subjective reference point and implements a logarithmic coding scheme convergently found in biological systems. Probing representations of years reveals a hierarchical construction process, where years evolve from basic numerical values in shallow layers to abstract temporal orientation in deep layers. Finally, using pre-trained embedding models, we found that the training corpus itself possesses an inherent, non-linear temporal structure, which provides the raw material for the model's internal construction. In discussion, we propose an experientialist perspective for understanding these findings, where the LLMs' cognition is viewed as a subjective construction of the external world by its internal representational system. This nuanced perspective implies the potential emergence of alien cognitive frameworks that humans cannot intuitively predict, pointing toward a direction for AI alignment that focuses on guiding internal constructions. Our code is available at https://TheOtherMind.github.io.

papers.title: Towards Explainable and Language-Agnostic LLMs: Symbolic Reverse Engineering of Language at Scale
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations be combined with bottom-up reverse engineering of language to create explainable and language-agnostic large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes combining symbolic representations with bottom-up reverse engineering of language to address the explainability and intensional context limitations of subsymbolic large language models, enabling the discovery of dimensions of word meanings and implicit ontology.
papers.conclusion: The ideal solution is to combine the advantages of bottom-up reverse engineering with explainable symbolic representations to overcome the limitations of current LLMs and achieve true language understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Large language models (LLMs) lack explainability due to their subsymbolic nature and non-invertible compositional computation, burying knowledge in meaningless microfeatures.
LLMs fail in intensional contexts and scope ambiguities that require commonsense knowledge, as demonstrated by examples with GPT-4.
Bottom-up reverse engineering of language at scale is viable, as evidenced by the success of LLMs, but it should be performed in a symbolic setting for explainability.
Symbolic reverse engineering using primitive relations (e.g., hasProp, inState) derived from context analysis can uncover dimensions of word meanings and the ontology implicit in language.
Concept similarity can be computed based on linguistic dimensions defined by primitive relations, providing a symbolic alternative to distributional semantics.
future_direction: How the symbolic dimensions of word meanings are used in language understanding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved a milestone that undenia-bly changed many held beliefs in artificial intelligence (AI). However, there remains many limitations of these LLMs when it comes to true language understanding, limitations that are a byproduct of the under-lying architecture of deep neural networks. Moreover, and due to their subsymbolic nature, whatever knowledge these models acquire about how language works will always be buried in billions of microfeatures (weights), none of which is meaningful on its own, making such models hopelessly unexplainable. To address these limitations, we suggest com-bining the strength of symbolic representations with what we believe to be the key to the success of LLMs, namely a successful bottom-up re-verse engineering of language at scale. As such we argue for a bottom-up reverse engineering of language in a symbolic setting. Hints on what this project amounts to have been suggested by several authors, and we discuss in some detail here how this project could be accomplished.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Improving Zero-Shot Translation by Disentangling Positional Information
papers.research_question: What is a main factor causing language-specific representations in multilingual NMT that hinders zero-shot translation, and how can it be alleviated?
papers.core_contribution: Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer improves zero-shot translation by reducing positional correspondence to input tokens, leading to more language-independent representations.
papers.conclusion: Positional correspondence to input tokens hinders zero-shot translation, and removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer alleviates this issue, leading to improved zero-shot performance and more language-independent representations.
papers.key_findings:
Removing residual connections in a middle encoder layer substantially improves zero-shot translation BLEU scores (up to 18.5 points gain).
The improvement is particularly prominent between related languages, where the proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation.
The approach allows easy integration of new languages, enabling zero-shot translation between the new language and all previously trained languages.
Analysis shows the proposed model creates encoder outputs with less positional correspondence and higher language independence, as measured by classification accuracy and SVCCA.
In low-resource, low lexical overlap settings (PMIndia), combining residual removal with variational dropout is essential for achieving reasonable zero-shot performance.
papers.limitation: The method requires additional regularization (variational dropout) to achieve reasonable zero-shot performance in low-resource settings with little lexical overlap (e.g., PMIndia).
papers.abstract: Multilingual neural machine translation has shown the capability of directly translating between language pairs unseen in training, i.e. zero-shot translation. Despite being conceptually attractive, it often suffers from low output quality. The difficulty of generalizing to new translation directions suggests the model representations are highly specific to those language pairs seen in training. We demonstrate that a main factor causing the language-specific representations is the positional correspondence to input tokens. We show that this can be easily alleviated by removing residual connections in an encoder layer. With this modification, we gain up to 18.5 BLEU points on zero-shot translation while retaining quality on supervised directions. The improvements are particularly prominent between related languages, where our proposed model outperforms pivot-based translation. Moreover, our approach allows easy integration of new languages, which substantially expands translation coverage. By thorough inspections of the hidden layer outputs, we show that our approach indeed leads to more language-independent representations.

papers.title: Exploring Multilingual Probing in Large Language Models: A Cross-Language Analysis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether other languages achieve comparable probing accuracy to English, whether they exhibit similar layer-wise behavioral patterns to English, and what the similarities are between probing vectors across different languages.
papers.core_contribution: The paper extends probing techniques to a multilingual context and reveals significant disparities in LLMs' performance and representational qualities between high-resource and low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and suggest that these models may not be learning deeper linguistic concepts effectively across all languages, especially low-resource ones.
papers.key_findings:
High-resource languages achieve higher probing accuracy than low-resource languages.
High-resource languages exhibit similar layer-wise trends to English, with accuracy improving in deeper layers, while low-resource languages show stable or only slight improvement.
Probing vectors of high-resource languages are more similar to each other, while low-resource languages have lower similarities among themselves and with high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Using machine translation to generate prompts and questions may introduce noise.
Only five open-source LLMs and two datasets are experimented with, limiting generalizability.
Only linear classifier probing is used; more sophisticated probing methods could offer deeper insights.
future_direction: Develop more equitable and effective multilingual language models that can better capture universal linguistic concepts.
Extend the research to multimodal models that incorporate visual and textual information.
Explore more sophisticated probing methods beyond linear classifiers.
papers.abstract: Probing techniques for large language models (LLMs) have primarily focused on English, overlooking the vast majority of the world's languages. In this paper, we extend these probing methods to a multilingual context, investigating the behaviors of LLMs across diverse languages. We conduct experiments on several open-source LLM models, analyzing probing accuracy, trends across layers, and similarities between probing vectors for multiple languages. Our key findings reveal: (1) a consistent performance gap between high-resource and low-resource languages, with high-resource languages achieving significantly higher probing accuracy; (2) divergent layer-wise accuracy trends, where high-resource languages show substantial improvement in deeper layers similar to English; and (3) higher representational similarities among high-resource languages, with low-resource languages demonstrating lower similarities both among themselves and with high-resource languages. These results highlight significant disparities in LLMs' multilingual capabilities and emphasize the need for improved modeling of low-resource languages.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: Towards a Deep Understanding of Multilingual End-to-End Speech Translation
papers.research_question: Does multilingual end-to-end speech translation exhibit properties similar to multilingual neural machine translation? How are learned representations distributed across languages and layers? Can the model predict linguistic typology features?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes multilingual end-to-end speech translation using SVCCA, finding that data quantity is more crucial than linguistic similarity for low-resource languages, and that encoder representations are effective for predicting phonetic typology features.
papers.conclusion: The amount of available data plays a significant role in limiting knowledge transfer across languages in multilingual speech translation. The model's encoder representations perform better on phonetic-related typology features compared to syntax features.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity loses its efficacy in multilingual speech translation when the training data for a specific language is limited.
Enhanced encoder representations and well-aligned audio-text data significantly improve translation quality, surpassing bilingual counterparts when training data is sufficient.
The encoder representations of multilingual speech translation demonstrate superior performance in predicting phonetic features in linguistic typology prediction.
Low-resource languages do not benefit from high-resource languages due to the lack of sufficient data to form language-specific sub-spaces.
Languages from the same language branch tend to cluster together in the representation space as layers deepen.
papers.limitation:
The quality of the LASER-based evaluation datasets may be compromised due to a lower threshold for semantic equivalence, potentially affecting SVCCA analysis reliability.
The analysis lacks a phonological perspective due to the absence of a reliable standard mapping between audio and phoneme, especially for low-resource languages.
future_direction: Addressing data scarcity in the multilingual setting to improve translation quality.
Improving the representation space for individual languages, especially for low-resource languages.
Learning high-quality representation spaces for low-resource languages with limited data to achieve linguistic fairness.
papers.abstract: In this paper, we employ Singular Value Canonical Correlation Analysis (SVCCA) to analyze representations learnt in a multilingual end-to-end speech translation model trained over 22 languages. SVCCA enables us to estimate representational similarity across languages and layers, enhancing our understanding of the functionality of multilingual speech translation and its potential connection to multilingual neural machine translation. The multilingual speech translation model is trained on the CoVoST 2 dataset in all possible directions, and we utilize LASER to extract parallel bitext data for SVCCA analysis. We derive three major findings from our analysis: (I) Linguistic similarity loses its efficacy in multilingual speech translation when the training data for a specific language is limited. (II) Enhanced encoder representations and well-aligned audio-text data significantly improve translation quality, surpassing the bilingual counterparts when the training data is not compromised. (III) The encoder representations of multilingual speech translation demonstrate superior performance in predicting phonetic features in linguistic typology prediction. With these findings, we propose that releasing the constraint of limited data for low-resource languages and subsequently combining them with linguistically related high-resource languages could offer a more effective approach for multilingual end-to-end speech translation.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: Layer by Layer: Uncovering Hidden Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the final layer always yield the best representation for downstream tasks, or can intermediate layers provide better representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that intermediate layers in language models often outperform final layers on downstream tasks, and introduces a unified information-theoretic framework to explain this phenomenon.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that intermediate layers often provide superior representations, challenging the default use of final layers, and provides a framework for understanding representation quality.
papers.key_findings:
Intermediate layers consistently outperform final layers across diverse architectures and tasks.
Autoregressive models exhibit a pronounced mid-layer compression valley, while masked or bidirectional models show milder changes.
The effect is domain-general, also observed in autoregressive vision transformers.
Chain-of-thought fine-tuning reshapes mid-layer entropy, preserving latent context for multi-step reasoning.
Intermediate layers strike a balance between information compression and signal preservation.
future_direction: Investigate the underlying causes of intermediate layer compression and do explicit finetuning to control compression.
papers.abstract: From extracting features to generating text, the outputs of large language models (LLMs) typically rely on the final layers, following the conventional wisdom that earlier layers capture only low-level cues. However, our analysis shows that intermediate layers can encode even richer representations, often improving performance on a range of downstream tasks. To explain and quantify these hidden-layer properties, we propose a unified framework of representation quality metrics based on information theory, geometry, and invariance to input perturbations. Our framework highlights how each layer balances information compression and signal preservation, revealing why mid-depth embeddings can exceed the last layer's performance. Through extensive experiments on 32 text-embedding tasks across various architectures (transformers, state-space models) and domains (language, vision), we demonstrate that intermediate layers consistently provide stronger features, challenging the standard view on final-layer embeddings and opening new directions on using mid-layer representations for more robust and accurate representations.

papers.title: Analysis and Visualization of Linguistic Structures in Large Language Models: Neural Representations of Verb-Particle Constructions in BERT
papers.research_question: Do the internal representations of BERT capture lexical semantics and phrase-level structure for verb-particle combinations? Which layers capture these phenomena, and can the activations be explained by usage-based theories?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that BERT's middle layers most effectively capture syntactic structures of verb-particle constructions, with significant variability in representational accuracy across different verb categories, challenging assumptions of uniform neural network processing.
papers.conclusion: The research underscores the capabilities of neural language models in processing linguistic sequences and provides a foundation for future investigations aimed at advancing their linguistic representational power.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's middle layers are most effective in capturing syntactic structures of verb-particle constructions.
There is significant variability in representational accuracy across different verb categories (e.g., 'agree', 'come', 'give').
The model captures the lexical unity of phrasal verbs (e.g., 'give up') and the compositionality of prepositional verbs (e.g., 'agree on').
Early and intermediate layers show strong clustering of constructions, while late layers show weak clustering, indicating less semantic unity.
The findings suggest a complex interplay between network architecture and linguistic representation.
future_direction: Further research into optimizing neural architectures for enhanced linguistic precision.
A multidisciplinary approach combining insights from computational linguistics, cognitive science, and neuroscience to develop models that better reflect human language understanding.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the internal representations of verb-particle combinations within transformer-based large language models (LLMs), specifically examining how these models capture lexical and syntactic nuances at different neural network layers. Employing the BERT architecture, we analyse the representational efficacy of its layers for various verb-particle constructions such as 'agree on', 'come back', and 'give up'. Our methodology includes a detailed dataset preparation from the British National Corpus, followed by extensive model training and output analysis through techniques like multi-dimensional scaling (MDS) and generalized discrimination value (GDV) calculations. Results show that BERT's middle layers most effectively capture syntactic structures, with significant variability in representational accuracy across different verb categories. These findings challenge the conventional uniformity assumed in neural network processing of linguistic elements and suggest a complex interplay between network architecture and linguistic representation. Our research contributes to a better understanding of how deep learning models comprehend and process language, offering insights into the potential and limitations of current neural approaches to linguistic analysis. This study not only advances our knowledge in computational linguistics but also prompts further research into optimizing neural architectures for enhanced linguistic precision.

papers.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements in their internal representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs compute and linearly represent the truth of factual statements in their internal activations, and introduces mass-mean probing as a simple method that identifies directions more causally implicated in model outputs.
papers.conclusion: The work finds evidence that LLMs linearly represent truth at scale, localizes these representations to specific hidden states, and shows that mass-mean probing is an effective method for identifying causally implicated truth directions.
papers.key_findings:
Linear representations of truth emerge with model scale, with larger models developing a more abstract notion of truth applicable across diverse inputs.
Truth representations are localized to a small group of hidden states (over the end-of-sentence punctuation token) in the residual stream.
Simple difference-in-mean (mass-mean) probes generalize as well as other probing techniques (logistic regression, CCS) for larger models and identify directions that are more causally effective in intervention experiments.
Training probes on datasets that include statements and their logical opposites (e.g., cities and neg cities) improves generalization, mitigating the effect of non-truth correlated features.
Probes trained solely on text likelihood (the likely dataset) perform poorly on datasets where truth and probability are anti-correlated, indicating the represented feature is not merely text probability.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on simple, uncontroversial factual statements, so cannot disambiguate truth from closely related features like 'commonly believed' or 'verifiable'.
Studies only models in the LLaMA-2 family, so results may not generalize to all LLMs.
future_direction: Why were interventions with mass-mean probe directions extracted from the likely dataset effective, despite these probes being inaccurate at classification?
Why did mass-mean probing with the cities+neg_cities training data perform poorly for the 70B model, while mass-mean probing with larger_than+smaller_than performed well?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have impressive capabilities, but are prone to outputting falsehoods. Recent work has developed techniques for inferring whether a LLM is telling the truth by training probes on the LLM's internal activations. However, this line of work is controversial, with some authors pointing out failures of these probes to generalize in basic ways, among other conceptual issues. In this work, we use high-quality datasets of simple true/false statements to study in detail the structure of LLM representations of truth, drawing on three lines of evidence: 1. Visualizations of LLM true/false statement representations, which reveal clear linear structure. 2. Transfer experiments in which probes trained on one dataset generalize to different datasets. 3. Causal evidence obtained by surgically intervening in a LLM's forward pass, causing it to treat false statements as true and vice versa. Overall, we present evidence that at sufficient scale, LLMs linearly represent the truth or falsehood of factual statements. We also show that simple difference-in-mean probes generalize as well as other probing techniques while identifying directions which are more causally implicated in model outputs.

papers.title: Language Arithmetics: Towards Systematic Language Neuron Identification and Manipulation
papers.research_question: How do language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs control language behavior, and can they be manipulated to steer model outputs across languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces language arithmetics, an additive neuron intervention method, to identify and manipulate language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs, showing that it can steer language generation and improve performance on downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: Our large-scale study demonstrates that language-specific neurons encode meaningful linguistic features that can be identified, analyzed, and manipulated to steer model behavior across languages. By employing a novel additive intervention method, we show that activating these neurons allows for generation language control and improves performance on various multilingual tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization.
Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting linguistic proximity.
Additive language arithmetics outperforms replacement-based methods for language forcing.
Activating target-language neurons improves performance on multilingual tasks like translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI.
Models exhibit internal 'fallback' mechanisms for language selection when dominant language neurons are deactivated.
papers.limitation:
Broader evaluation across more diverse downstream settings is needed.
Quality and fluency of forced outputs across languages, especially low-resource ones, remain underexplored.
Analysis focuses on isolated neurons, overlooking distributed representations and circuits.
Computational constraints limited some experiments to smaller models.
future_direction: Investigate the interactions and dependencies between neurons to understand network-level mechanisms supporting multilingual processing.
More detailed investigation of language fallback dynamics.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong multilingual abilities, yet the neural mechanisms behind language-specific processing remain unclear. We analyze language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, and Aya-Expanse-8B & 32B across 21 typologically diverse languages, identifying neurons that control language behavior. Using the Language Activation Probability Entropy (LAPE) method, we show that these neurons cluster in deeper layers, with non-Latin scripts showing greater specialization. Related languages share overlapping neurons, reflecting internal representations of linguistic proximity. Through language arithmetics, i.e. systematic activation addition and multiplication, we steer models to deactivate unwanted languages and activate desired ones, outperforming simpler replacement approaches. These interventions effectively guide behavior across five multilingual tasks: language forcing, translation, QA, comprehension, and NLI. Manipulation is more successful for high-resource languages, while typological similarity improves effectiveness. We also demonstrate that cross-lingual neuron steering enhances downstream performance and reveal internal "fallback" mechanisms for language selection when neurons are progressively deactivated. Our code is made publicly available at https://github.com/d-gurgurov/Language-Neurons-Manipulation.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: Learning Music Helps You Read: Using Transfer to Study Linguistic Structure in Language Models
